articles.title: Canadian Smarties, honeycomb bars and 12 international candies way better than Snickers
articles.summary: Forget the familiar favorites and try these sweets from around the world – from caffeine-boosted chocolate drops to dragonfruit gummies – available before Halloween. ‘Tastes like Play-Doh’: the best (and worst) chocolate bars.
body: Welcome to Filter finds, a series where Guardian staff and Filter contributors share the things we love most – and think you might, too.

Every October, we set out to rot our teeth on the same high fructose corn-syrup candies. Twizzlers! Snickers! Almond Joy! But these words have no meaning outside of the US. Beyond the hegemony of Hershey, Mars and Mondelēz lies a world of honeycomb bars, caffeine-boosted chocolate drops and dragonfruit gummies that the American mind simply can’t comprehend … though maybe our stomachs can.

We asked our Guardian colleagues for their favorite candy from around the world – be they childhood treats or souvenirs picked up through travels abroad – that we don’t need a plane ticket to try ourselves. They’re all available online, and yes, we checked: as of publication, they will all arrive before Halloween.
points: Forget the familiar favorites and try these sweets from around the world – from caffeine-boosted chocolate drops to dragonfruit gummies – available before Halloween.

articles.title: Curiosity, atonement or a score to settle? Why – and how – people get through their high school reunions
articles.summary: Reunions can be riotous, scandalous or just plain awkward. Experts and attendees share how to go in prepared. Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email. Mike walked into his 20th high school reunion with a mission.
body: Some may relish the chance to reconnect with former friends, a former life and even a former self, but for many they are a potential hellscape, where adolescent humiliations are revived in front of a group of rapidly ageing peers.

Mike, who attended an all-boys’ school in Melbourne’s comfortable eastern suburbs, belonged to the latter group. Though he wasn’t there for vengeance. He was there to apologise. For years, he’d felt regret about the homophobic bullying a friend had faced at school. Although Mike never targeted the boy himself, he “always felt guilty about not doing enough”.
He knew he couldn’t change the past, but he hoped to clear his conscience and apologise for not intervening.

The pair did connect, and atonements were made. Mike, though, left with new laments. “It was a fumbly conversation that ended up with him consoling me about not having to feel guilty. I felt like a bit of a dick, accidentally getting an old friend who’d experienced genuinely horrific bullying to walk me through my feelings.”
points: Reunions can be riotous, scandalous or just plain awkward.

articles.title: Fridge or not? What’s the best way to store bread?
articles.summary: Our experts have some airtight advice on stopping your loaf from going stale – and even freshening it up again – but whatever you do, keep it out of the fridge. What’s the best way to store bread? Beeswax wraps, plastic bags, fridge – I’ve tried everything except a bread bin.
body: To combat this, Handschuh stores her loaf at room temperature in a greaseproof paper bag (ie, the one you bring it home in): “That’s probably the best way – no plastic. And, yes, you can use beeswax wrap, but that’s expensive and you shouldn’t have to go and buy some just for storing bread.”

A paper bag is also Rachel Morgan’s preference: “I’d avoid a bread bin, though,” says the co-founder of Twelve Triangles in Edinburgh. “That can trap moisture, so the bread gets a bit sweaty, which softens the crust and encourages mould.”

Reheating is your gateway to regaining freshness: “Warming bread enables the water to evaporate and for the starch to reactivate,” Handschuh says. So, if your bread is a couple of days’ old, “stick it in the oven for five to 10 minutes, and it should stay fresh for a day or two longer”.

articles.title: ‘How green are our valleys?’: in the footsteps of miners on south Wales’s new forest trail
articles.summary: The first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villages. Bracken and heather ripple across the plateau.
body: I’m hiking the new Llwybr Coedwig Cymru Trail, or Wales Forest Trail. Running from Porthkerry Park, near Barry, to Pont Walby, close to Glynneath, this 50-mile (80km) pilot route is the first section of what the National Forest for Wales hopes will eventually be a trail linking woodlands across the length and breadth of Wales: a sylvan counterpart to the Wales Coast Path.

My father grew up in one of the valleys’ mining villages and, when I visited relatives there as a child, the disconnection of those post-industrial communities from the wild hills that loomed above them was striking. Mountain bikers have long discovered the region’s potential, but walkers still tend to head for the more obvious trails that wind through the national parks or along the coast. This pilot trail seems a good excuse to explore untapped footpaths.

With the sea behind me, I set off from the oak leaf sculpture that marks the trail’s start. The viaduct ahead once carried coal to Barry docks, but today it stands over Caffe Matteo, busy with dog walkers sipping cappuccinos. Leaving them behind, I cross the park between the soft greens of birch and oak trees.

articles.title: 7 of the Best Birdwatching Travel Destinations Around the World
articles.summary: Travelers might plan their next adventure around all manner of things: a buzzy chef, a sports event, an art exhibition... Would it be so absurd to plan a trip around a bird?
body: Want to try it for yourself? Here, find seven destination ideas that take more itinerary inspiration from the Merlin app than they do from the Michelin guide.

We’ve seen flamingos elsewhere in the Mediterranean, including in the Camargue, outside of Avignon. But in Sicily, an adventure to spot a flamingo also brings an outdoorsy edge to a few days of Baroque villages and beach time, while introducing us to an underexplored stretch of coastline—not to mention these holes in the rocky coast where, Corso tells us, archaeologists think the Romans used to torture prisoners of war with carnivorous eels.

Everyone who can go on an African safari should go on an African safari—it’s a trip with an incredible power to recalibrate one’s perspective. But there are multiple kinds of safari-goers. My husband and I realized quickly we were different. We weren’t seeing eye to eye with the big cat photography buffs: Lions came and went, but we nearly jumped out of the Jeep the one time we saw a Secretarybird, and we would’ve been contented to spend 45 minutes sitting under an acacia tree watching a giant Verreaux's eagle-owl bat its freaky pink eyelids.

articles.title: In Her Sequel to 'Big Little Lies,' Liane Moriarty Shines a Light on Suburban Australia's Dark Side
articles.summary: The lifelong Sydneysider on why her home country is the only place that her novels could be set—and how it felt to see them translated to California on the silver screen.
body: “I don't actually think a sense of place is one of my strengths. I find dialogue and character come easily to me, but I'm not somebody who describes scenery particularly well, and I have a very poor memory about anywhere that I've visited. I remember the people that I meet, but I find it hard to remember the actual places, which is why I always set all my books in Australia—I can literally look out the window and see where I am!

Definitely with Big Little Lies and Big Little Truths, the lives of these characters seem amazing, but when you dig deeper there are all these threats. I'm always interested in characters who look like they've got it all together and perhaps they don't, and how real people present themselves to the world versus what's really going on. If you've ever developed a friendship, you might have an instant first impression and then as you get to know them, you realize, oh, actually, they're this sort of person. And in the same way it's interesting to have a really beautiful setting and then explore the dark things that can happen behind closed doors.
points: The lifelong Sydneysider on why her home country is the only place that her novels could be set—and how it felt to see them translated to California on the silver screen.

articles.title: Brands Prepare for More Looting as Further Protests Are Planned Across Europe
articles.summary: Protests are on the rise in Europe as citizens push back against dire cost of living and education conditions. Store looters are exacerbating the situation.
body: Luxury is on high alert in Europe. Hundreds of stores have been looted in Paris and other French cities, including Saint Laurent, Celine, Dior and Louis Vuitton, as looters took advantage of the cost of living and inequality protests that have gathered both students and members of France’s Yellow Vests movement.

Calls for more strikes and demonstrations over the next three weekends are bubbling up. In Milan, some stores have shuttered and troops have been dispatched in anticipation of protests in the Italian fashion capital, while demonstrations have also materialized in towns across the country. More protests unraveled in Spain, Belgium and Portugal over the past few weeks, with tensions escalating since the weekend.

articles.title: Kate Middleton’s New Favorite Accessory? This Quilted Chanel Bag
articles.summary: Kate Middleton, the Princess of Wales, welcomed the Sultan of Oman to London in her favourite Alexander McQueen coat—as well as her latest Chanel bag obsession.
body: With a busy calendar of royal engagements, it’s no wonder the Princess of Wales is a fan of rewearing failsafe looks. It’s this practical (and sustainable) approach to official-duty dressing that sees her return to her favourite British labels time after time, with Emilia Wickstead, Burberry and Alexander McQueen in her forever wardrobe rotation. Case in point: this afternoon, when Catherine welcomed the Sultan of Oman to Windsor Castle, she wore a much-loved Alexander McQueen coat, accessorized with a classic quilted Chanel bag.

The Princess of Wales was first seen wearing the “squashed” bag back in the spring, when she carried a crumpled Chanel flap bag to the enthronement ceremony for Dame Sarah Mullally, co-signing one of the season’s most talked-about trends in the process. Today, the investment accessory paired perfectly with her bottle-green coat, previously worn at the Irish Guards’ St Patrick’s Day parade.
